description: I am an independent participant passionate about space science, technology, innovation, and problem-solving. I enjoy exploring new ideas and developing creative solutions to real-world challenges. My interests include astronomy, space exploration, artificial intelligence, and technology. I am excited to take on this challenge independently, learn new things, and contribute innovative ideas to the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary: Echoes in Orbit is an interactive digital storytelling project by Team VYOMNEXA that brings to life the journeys, scientific discoveries, and final resting places of NASA's retired space assets. Every major space breakthrough is built on the legacy of earlier missions. Yet once their primary objectives end, many spacecraft, rovers, and satellites are decommissioned, left in graveyard orbits, or intentionally crashed into planetary surfaces. Their data remains in archives, but their stories are often forgotten by the general public. To address the challenge, we transformed technical mission archives into human-centered, first-person narratives for three iconic missions: Cassini's grand finale into Saturn, the Opportunity rover's 15-year Martian marathon, and the Spitzer Space Telescope. Using real NASA mission timelines and imagery, we show what each machine discovered, why its mission ended, and how its hardware paved the way for modern exploration. The project is important because it makes complex space science accessible to students and space enthusiasts, and it teaches the next generation about mission engineering, space sustainability, and the enduring legacy of space exploration. Our storybook and presentation pair authentic NASA data with clear, engaging visuals so that anyone can follow each mission from launch to its final moments.
details:
Echoes in Orbit is a visual storytelling project by Team VYOMNEXA about NASA's retired space missions. It turns technical mission archives into short first-person stories told by the spacecraft themselves: Cassini's grand finale into Saturn, the Opportunity rover's 15-year journey on Mars, and the Spitzer Space Telescope. Each story covers what the mission discovered, why it ended, and how it paved the way for modern exploration.

Benefits and impact: The project makes mission history easy to read and remember for students and space enthusiasts. It teaches mission engineering, space sustainability, and the legacy of earlier missions, so retired spacecraft are not forgotten once their data goes into archives.

Tools: We used the NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA), the NASA Image and Video Library, and the NASA Solar System Exploration Archives to verify mission timelines and facts. A storybook PDF and a slide presentation were created with the help of AI tools (Super Intelligence).

Creativity: Instead of a technical report, each mission "speaks" for itself, with a consistent visual style, a clear legacy line for each mission, and an epilogue connecting all three stories.

Factors considered: factual accuracy checked against NASA sources, accessibility for a general audience, clear and simple writing, public links that need no login, and no use of NASA logos or branding.
